title: Increased spread of global flash droughts threatens vegetation productivity resilience
abstract: Flash drought (faster-developing drought) has been pervasively intensified, posing detrimental constraints on vegetation productivity. However, the potential expansion of flash droughts from flash drought hotspots to non-hotspots and its associated risks to vegetation productivity remain unknown. Furthermore, the divergence in the underlying drivers governing vegetation productivity responses to flash and slow droughts (slower-developing droughts) is unclear. We quantify the dominant drivers underlying vegetation productivity resilience (the departure of productivity anomalies after drought effect to the long-term mean) to both flash and slow droughts. There exhibits significantly lower productivity resilience to flash drought at flash drought hotspots than non-hotspots (Δ = -0.07 ± 0.02, t = -3.25, p < 0.001). The productivity resilience to flash drought is more sensitive to the same reduction in productivity anomaly and intensified climate stress than slow drought. Carbon dioxide fertilization effect exerts the greatest positive effect on productivity resilience to both flash and slow droughts, although that effect is smaller under flash droughts. Our study underscores the limited global ecosystem resilience to the intensification and spread of flash droughts.
problem: The potential expansion of flash droughts from hotspots to non-hotspots and its risks to vegetation are unknown, and the divergence in underlying drivers governing how vegetation productivity resilience responds to flash versus slow droughts is unclear.
method: The authors propose a method that uses soil moisture data to identify flash droughts and a multivariate indicator to define hotspots, then applies random forest models to quantify and attribute the drivers of vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts across these regions.
task: The task is to characterize the spatiotemporal intensification of global flash droughts and identify the divergent drivers of vegetation productivity resilience in response to both flash and slow droughts.
innovation: This paper reveals that intensifying flash droughts are spreading globally from hotspots to non-hotspots, threatening vegetation productivity resilience more than slow droughts due to greater sensitivity to climate stress and a diminished CO2 fertilization effect.

We first quantified the spatiotemporal patterns in the occurrence of flash and slow droughts from 1950 to 2023. The flash and slow droughts were determined by the decline in onset speed, with flash drought having no less than 5% in percentile for each pentad and slow drought having at least one pentad with the decline rate of less than 5% in percentile (see Methods). The counts, onset speed and severity of flash drought exhibited great spatial heterogeneity. There exhibited a larger number of more severe flash drought events in the western and southern parts of the Amazon, the western Sahel and tropical Southeast Asia (Figure 1a – c).

We quantified and compared the GPP resilience to flash and slow droughts. The GPP resilience is quantified by the difference between mean GPP anomalies within two years after the drought and the multi- year mean growing season GPP. Global GPP showed lower resilience to flash drought than slow drought (Δ = -0.012 ± 0.004, t = -2.74, p < 0.01), and regions with lower GPP resilience to flash drought than that to slow drought are mainly located in North America, central Asia, eastern Europe and central Australia (Figure 3a).

In this study, vegetation productivity was investigated via a daily gross primary productivity (GPP) dataset, which was directly obtained from FluxSat (2001 – 2019) (https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/catalog/ornl-cloud-fluxsat-gpp-fpar-1835-2) 43.
We also used 4-day solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) data from the CSIF dataset (2001 – 2019) (https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/CSIF/6387494) for supplementary analyses 44.

The CSIF dataset is produced based on SIF retrievals from OCO-2 and surface reflectance data derived from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) onboard the Terra and Aqua satellites (0.05 degrees) 44.
